newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Shenzhen B shares end down on controls on locals.
newsitem.headline: Shenzhen B shares end down on controls on locals.

text.p: Shenzhen's B share index closed sharply lower on Wednesday due to profit-taking and a new crackdown by securities regulators on mainland Chinese buying B shares, brokers said.
The B index fell 7.42 points, or 3.83 percent, to close at 186.45 after hitting an intraday low of 175.39 on turnover of HK$509.83 million against Tuesday's HK$724.79 million.
All 43 Shenzhen-listed B counters were traded, with 40 falling and three rising.

Brokers said most local brokerages had received official notices from the Shenzhen Securities Management Office (SSMO), the local regulatory body, ordering them to stop accepting B share trading accounts from domestic investors unless their funds come from outside mainland China.

A senior official at the SSMO confirmed the notice, saying that it had been released recently at the urging of the Foreign Exchange Management Bureau under the People's Bank of China and the China Securities Regulatory Commission.

To buy Shenzhen-listed B shares, a domestic investor must have a copy of an overseas resident's passport, a notarised letter saying the Chinese is entrusted by the foreigner to buy B shares and a certificate proving the money used to buy B shares comes from outside mainland China, the official said.
Many Chinese have recently entered the B market using foreigners' passports but their own HK dollars, brokers said.
"The inflow of fresh money into the market will definitely slow with the implementation of the policy, but many Chinese can still enter the market by some means or other," a broker said.
Sustained profit-taking added to Wednesday's retreat, brokers said.
"The B index has risen about 100 percent over the past several weeks and needs to consolidate," one analyst said.
Lionda was the worst performer, diving HK$0.55, or 8.94 percent, to HK$5.60 on trade of 992,560 shares.
Changan traded the most on volume of 5.89 million shares and lost HK$0.38 to HK$5.80. SEG bucked the trend with a gain of HK$0.38 to HK$7.88 after 4.72 million shares were traded.
The A share index climbed 11.29 points, or 2.32 percent, to 498.45 due in part due to institutional demand for expensive issues, brokers said.
Turnover was 14.86 billion yuan compared with 14.01 billion the previous session.
The composite index ended up 2.00 percent at 473.02.
Xinjiang Huitong surged 3.57 yuan, or 18.00 percent, to 23.40 yuan.
